speaker: Doctor
text: I see you have yellowish coloring in your skin and eyes, which suggests jaundice; have you noticed any severe abdominal pain, fever, or changes in your urine or stool color recently? This history will help me understand if this is due to liver failure, bile duct obstruction, or another condition.

speaker: Patient
text: 20-year-old male. The patient was previously healthy and has been brought to the emergency department due to agitation over the past 24 hours. Family members have noticed a yellowish coloring of his skin and eyes over the past week. The patient has a history of occasional cocaine and ecstasy use, and drinks alcohol socially on weekends. The patient also admits to high-risk sexual behaviors without using appropriate protection.

speaker: Doctor
text: That history is concerning; given your recent drug use and high-risk behaviors, could you tell me if you have experienced any nausea, vomiting, or confusion alongside these symptoms? REQUEST TEST: Liver function panel (AST, ALT, Bilirubin, Alkaline Phosphatase, PT/INR).

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: AST: 600 IU/L (elevated), ALT: 650 IU/L (elevated), Bilirubin: 25 mg/dL (elevated), Alkaline Phosphatase: Not Available, PT/INR: INR 1.5 (elevated).

speaker: Doctor
text: Thank you for those results; the significantly elevated AST and ALT with high bilirubin and prolonged INR indicate severe hepatocellular injury and coagulopathy. Given your history of ecstasy and cocaine use, have you experienced any seizures, hallucinations, or memory lapses in the days leading up to this admission? REQUEST TEST: Ammonia level, Arterial Blood Gas.

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Ammonia: 185 µmol/L (elevated), Arterial Blood Gas: pH 7.28, pCO2 28 mmHg, pO2 88 mmHg, HCO3- 18 mEq/L (Metabolic Acidosis)

speaker: Doctor
text: The combination of severe hepatocellular injury, high ammonia, and metabolic acidosis alongside your history of cocaine use is highly concerning for hepatorenal syndrome or severe acetaminophen toxicity. Have you been taking any over-the-counter pain relievers, specifically Tylenol or cold medications, in the last few days? REQUEST TEST: Acetaminophen level, Creatinine, BUN, and Electrolytes.

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Acetaminophen level: Undetectable, Creatinine: 2.1 mg/dL (elevated), BUN: 28 mg/dL (elevated), Electrolytes: Sodium 128 mEq/L (low), Potassium 3.9 mEq/L, Chloride 98 mEq/L, CO2 18 mEq/L.

speaker: Doctor
text: Given the undetectable acetaminophen, your rising creatinine, and the specific history of ecstasy and cocaine use, did you experience any muscle pain, dark urine, or difficulty passing stool recently? REQUEST TEST: Creatine Kinase (CK), Urinalysis for myoglobin, and Coagulation Profile. REQUEST IMAGES: Abdominal Ultrasound.

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Creatine Kinase (CK): Not Available, Urinalysis for myoglobin: Not Available, Coagulation Profile: INR 1.5 (elevated), PT: Not Available, Abdominal Ultrasound: Not Available.

speaker: Doctor
text:
DIAGNOSIS READY: Acute Liver Failure secondary to Acute Fatty Liver of Pregnancy (mimic) or severe Ischemic Hepatitis with rhabdomyolysis; however, given the undetectable acetaminophen and cocaine/ecstasy use, the primary working diagnosis is Acute Liver Failure likely due to Cocaine-induced vasospasm (Hepatic Infarction) and/or Ischemic Hepatitis, complicated by Acute Kidney Injury and Metabolic Encephalopathy. The markedly elevated Bilirubin and AST/ALT with undetectable acetaminophen and elevated CK suggest a toxic-metabolic or ischemic etiology over viral or acetaminophen toxicity. Further imaging is critical to rule out biliary obstruction or focal infarction.

REQUEST IMAGES: Abdominal CT with contrast.
DIAGNOSIS READY: Acute Liver Failure due to Cocaine-induced Hepatic Infarction and Ischemic
